title: The Six Demon Embryos and Devaki's Conception
story:
News came to Kamsa, king of Mathura, from the sage Narada — the wandering seer who carried tidings between the worlds — and it turned his fear into a plan. Kamsa was to die at the hands of a child of his sister Devaki. The warning was not new, for a prophecy at Devaki's wedding had already promised it, but to hear it spoken plainly left him no room for hope. So he did what a frightened king does: he resolved to destroy every child Devaki might bear, beginning not at the birth but at the very beginning.

He shut Devaki and her husband Vasudeva inside the palace prison, set warders over them, and ordered his ministers to count the months from the first sign of a child, so that nothing could slip past him. Vasudeva was watched day and night, told nothing, allowed nothing. Even an adverse destiny, Kamsa told his ministers, could be turned propitious by the right rites, the right medicines, by care and devotion. It was the reasoning of a man who believed his fear could be outworked.

But beneath the fear lay a design that Kamsa could not see. Long before, six demons — the Saragarbhas, sons of Kalanemi and grandsons of Hiranyakashipu, a tyrant of ages past — had won a boon from Brahma through hard penance: no god or man could harm them, no weapon could cut them, no curse could touch them. Because they had asked Brahma for the boon instead of him, their grandfather Hiranyakashipu had turned on them in fury and cursed them: they would be born from Devaki, one after another, and Kamsa would kill them as soon as they came into the world. So the children Kamsa meant to destroy were not the innocent victims of chance he took them for. They were six ancient enemies, walking toward a death that had been spoken over them long before.

Vishnu saw all of this. He went down into the nether regions — the dark worlds beneath the earth — where the six demons lay in a death-like sleep, and he entered their dreams. One by one he took hold of their life-breaths and gave them into the keeping of Sleep, commanding her to place them in Devaki's womb, in their order. The first six would be born and pass on to the house of Death, and Kamsa's fear, which believed it was averting fate, would only be serving it. Vishnu gave Sleep her other tasks as well: in the seventh month of Devaki's seventh conception, she was to lift that elder brother from Devaki into the womb of Rohini, Vasudeva's other wife — the child who would grow up known as Balarama. Sleep herself, who would be called Yogamaya, was to be born on earth as the daughter of Yashoda, Nanda's wife.

Then came the moment itself. Vishnu entered the heart of Vasudeva, and from Vasudeva the Lord passed into Devaki — a portion of the divine taking its place in her womb. Devaki, who now carried the support of the whole world within her, began to glow with a light that filled the prison. The guards who watched her could not say what had changed, only that the room seemed brighter, and that her face shone as it had never shone before.

Kamsa came to look at his sister, and what he saw stopped him at the door. The woman before him was so bright that he saw in her, plainly, the presence of the very one who would destroy him. In that instant he knew his death had come near, that it rested in his own sister's womb, and that the moment to act was this one. But he stayed his hand. To strike with such cruelty, he told himself, would be the act of a man already dead, and the child, once born, would be easier to destroy than the mother who carried it. So he turned away from the cruelest thought and let her be. He sat and lay down and stood and ate and walked the earth, waiting and watching her with a terrible patience, certain he could still undo what had been done.
reflection: Kamsa's restraint is not mercy but strategy: he spares Devaki because he means to kill the child later. The episode shows how fear, once it becomes a plan, no longer needs to be told what to do; it devises its own cruelties and calls them prudence.
tradition_note: The account of the six demon embryos cursed by Hiranyakashipu comes from the Harivamsha and the Vishnu Purana. The Bhagavata Purana (10.2.15-23) tells Devaki's conception and radiance, and Kamsa's decision to stay his hand, without the six-embryo backstory.
next_story_tease: Before the child was born, the gods themselves would come down to praise him where he waited.
hero_scene: Devaki glowing with an unearthly radiance in the prison as Kamsa, halted at the door, sees in her face the presence of his own destroyer and stays his hand.
visual_elements: Devaki radiant with the unborn Lord's light
Kamsa at the cell door, stopped mid-step
a mood of awe and held breath
